problem: Find a point that satisfies the mean value theorem for $f(x,y,z)={x}^{2}-{y}^{2}$ on the line segment $\overset{―}{AB},$ where the position vectors of $A$ and $B$ are $a=⟨-1,0,3⟩$ and $b=⟨0,4,0⟩,$ respectively.
worked_solution:
The mean value theorem states that if $f(x,y,z)$ is differentiable at each point on the line segment $\overset{―}{AB},$ then there exists a point $C\in \overset{―}{AB}$ with position vector $c$ such that

$$
f(b)-f(a)=∇f(c)·(b-a).
$$

Notice that $f(x,y,z)={x}^{2}-{y}^{2}$ is differentiable at each point on the line segment $\overset{―}{AB}.$ So, we can apply the mean value theorem.

Substituting $a=⟨-1,0,3⟩$ and $b=⟨0,4,0⟩$ into the above expression, we get

$$
\begin{aligned}f(0,4,0)-f(-1,0,3) & =∇f(c)\cdot (⟨0,4,0⟩-⟨-1,0,3⟩) \\ -16-1 & =∇f(c)\cdot ⟨1,4,-3⟩ \\ -17 & =∇f(c)\cdot ⟨1,4,-3⟩.\end{aligned}
$$

Computing $∇f$ and evaluating at $c=⟨{c}_{1},{c}_{2},{c}_{3}⟩,$ we get 

$$
\begin{aligned}∇f & =⟨2x,-2y,0⟩ \\ ∇f(c) & =⟨2{c}_{1},-2{c}_{2},0⟩.\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore, we get

$$
\begin{aligned}-17 & =∇f(c)\cdot ⟨1,4,-3⟩ \\ -17 & =⟨2{c}_{1},-2{c}_{2},0⟩\cdot ⟨1,4,-3⟩ \\ -17 & =2{c}_{1}-8{c}_{2}.\end{aligned}
$$

Now, we use the fact that $C$ lies on $\overset{―}{AB}.$ So, let's first find the equation of the line.

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{x-(-1)}{1} & =\frac{y-0}{4}=\frac{z-3}{(-3)} \\ x+1 & =\frac{y}{4}=\frac{3-z}{3}\end{aligned}
$$

Parametrizing the line, we get

$$
x=t-1,\,y=4t,\,z=3-3t,\,0\le t\le 1.
$$

Since $c=⟨{c}_{1},{c}_{2},{c}_{3}⟩$ satisfies the equation of the line, we have

$$
{c}_{1}=t-1,\,{c}_{2}=4t,\,{c}_{3}=3-3t.
$$

Substituting the above in the equation $2{c}_{1}-8{c}_{2}=-17,$ we get

$$
\begin{aligned}2(t-1)-8(4t) & =-17 \\ 2t-2-32t & =-17 \\ -30t & =-15 \\ t & =\frac{1}{2}.\end{aligned}
$$

We can now find the values of ${c}_{1},$ ${c}_{2},$ and ${c}_{3}.$ This gives

$$
\begin{aligned}{c}_{1} & =\frac{1}{2}-1=-\frac{1}{2}, \\ {c}_{2} & =4(\frac{1}{2})=2, \\ {c}_{3} & =3-3(\frac{1}{2})=\frac{3}{2}.\end{aligned}
$$

Finally, the coordinates of $C$ are $(-\frac{1}{2},2,\frac{3}{2}).$
